Alright, let me think this through the way I always do, field by field.

---

I'm 71 this year. My back isn't what it was, and it's just me and the old lady at home now — the kids are in town, they come back for the wheat harvest if they can get off work. 10.5 mu isn't much but it feels like plenty when you're doing it with two pairs of hands. Well, one and a half pairs.

**Winter wheat — all 10.5 mu, like always**

I put wheat on everything in the winter. That's how we've always done it around here. I'll plant around the cold dew, maybe October 10th or a little after, depending on when the summer crops come off and when it rains. Same seed as last year — the one the agricultural supply shop sells, I think they call it Jimai-something, my neighbor Old Wang gets the same. Some of the younger fellows are buying those expensive new varieties but at 50 yuan a mu for seed I'm not going to gamble.

For fertilizer, before planting I put down one bag of compound 15-15-15 for every two mu — that's what my father did, that's what I do. Then at jointing, when the wheat starts standing up tall in March, I topdress urea. Usually about half a bag per mu if the wheat looks yellow, a bit less if it looks green and happy. Last year I used maybe 15-16 kg of nitrogen per mu all told, and I got a decent harvest, so I'll do the same.

Watering — I water before winter to settle the roots, then at jointing when I topdress (the water carries the fertilizer in), and once more at grain-filling if May is dry. Three times is enough most years. The well pump costs money and I watch the meter. My neighbor Liu waters four or five times but he's got more land and a son who helps.

I'll spray herbicide once in spring when the weeds start up. Sometimes the aphids come bad and I'll spray for those too. I hire the big combine for harvest — 60 yuan a mu, but there's no way I'm cutting 10 mu of wheat by hand at my age.

Last year I got about 420 kg a mu. I'll count on the same.

**Summer — splitting the land between maize and millet**

After the wheat comes off in June, I have to get the summer crops in fast, within a week if I can. I split my land — about 6 mu to maize, 4.5 mu to millet. Maize brings more money per mu if the weather holds, but millet is my insurance. Millet doesn't mind dry weather, doesn't need much fertilizer, and it's what my wife and I eat for porridge all winter. We always keep millet — old habit, good habit.

*Maize (6 mu):* I buy the hybrid seed, no saving seed for maize, everyone knows that. About 60 yuan a mu for seed. I hire the planter to come right after the wheat is off — 20 yuan a mu, done in half a day. For fertilizer I put down compound at planting and then urea at the big whorl stage, maybe 13-14 kg N per mu total. Water once or twice if July-August is dry. Spray herbicide once when the weeds come up between rows. Hire the combine again in September. Last year I got maybe 470 kg a mu. I'll count on 450.

*Millet (4.5 mu):* Millet is old-people's crop now, most of the young ones don't grow it. I have seed from last year's good patch — I always set aside the nicest heads. Saves me money. I plant late June, a bit after the maize. Fertilizer is light — maybe half a bag of compound per mu and a little urea later, maybe 7-8 kg N per mu total. Millet doesn't want rich soil, makes it grow too tall and fall over. Usually I don't water millet at all unless it's a terrible dry spell. Weeding is the hard part — I'll spray a little herbicide and my wife and I hand-pull what's left. Harvest is late September, we cut it ourselves with sickles, a few rows a day. Slow but that's how it is. 250 kg a mu is a good year.

**On money and labor**

The whole year I figure I'll spend around 8,000 yuan on inputs — seed, fertilizer, water, chemicals, machinery hire. That's the money I have to put up front from last year's savings and what I get when I sell the wheat. If prices on fertilizer jump again like they did a couple years ago, I'll cut back on the topdressing, not on the base. The base fertilizer matters most, that's what my old neighbor taught me forty years ago and he was right.

Labor-wise, I hire machinery for the heavy work — plowing, planting, combine harvest. Everything else my wife and I do ourselves: watering, spraying, the millet harvest. Probably 50-60 days of our own labor across the year, and maybe 15 days worth of hired machinery.

I'm not trying to get rich at 71. I'm trying to keep the land productive, eat good food, and have enough left over that I'm not a burden on my kids. Same as every year.
